analysis.one_liner: Repeals federal income, payroll, and estate taxes and replaces them with a 23% national sales tax.
analysis.headline: Despite 76 Republican cosponsors, the bill received no hearing, markup, or vote beyond its first-day referral to the Ways and Means Committee.
analysis.plain_summary: The FairTax would abolish the federal income tax, the Social Security and Medicare payroll taxes, and the estate and gift taxes, replacing all of them with a single 23% national sales tax on nearly everything consumers buy new, including rent on housing. Every lawful-resident family would get a monthly rebate covering the tax on poverty-level spending, and states would collect the tax for the Treasury. The IRS would lose its funding after 2019, and the sales tax would automatically end if the constitutional amendment allowing an income tax were not repealed within seven years.
analysis.who_benefits: The clearest gainers would be high-income households and heirs: the income tax on wages, salaries, dividends, and capital gains, plus the estate tax, would all disappear, and purchases made for investment purposes would be untaxed [S2] [S3]. Supporters argue that working families gain too, because payroll tax withholding ends and the monthly rebate covers the tax on poverty-level consumption, making effective rates near zero for the poorest households [S2] [S3]. Businesses would shed income tax filing and compliance, and state governments would be paid to collect the federal tax [S2].
analysis.who_benefits_short: High earners, heirs, and large estates

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the federal income tax, Social Security and Medicare payroll taxes, and the estate and gift taxes, and replaces them with one 23% sales tax on consumption [S2] [S3].

Provides a monthly 'Family Consumption Allowance' rebate to every lawful-resident family, equal to 23% of the federal poverty-level spending amount for that family's size, paid by the Social Security Administration [S2] [S3].
Ends income tax filing and withholding entirely, and forbids any funding for IRS operations after fiscal year 2019 [S2].
Shifts collection to the states: any state with a sales tax can administer the federal tax and keep a 0.25% administration fee [S2] [S3].
Contains a self-destruct clause: the sales tax terminates unless the Sixteenth Amendment is repealed within seven years, so the income tax could not simply be restored on top of it [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Consumers would pay the tax at the register on nearly all new goods and services, including rent on real property; because the 23% is calculated on the total price including the tax, that equals roughly a 30-cent markup on every dollar of pre-tax price. Families above the poverty line would pay according to how much they spend, not earn, and retirees spending money they already saved and paid income tax on would be taxed a second time as they spend it. Sellers would take on registration, collection, segregation accounts, and bonding duties, offset by a small administration credit.

drawbacks.text: A consumption tax takes a larger share of income from families who must spend most of what they earn; the rebate shields only poverty-level spending, so a middle-income family spending well beyond the poverty line pays the full 23% on everything above it [S2] [S3].

Income from savings, capital gains, and estates would be entirely untaxed, and property bought for investment purposes would be exempt, shifting the tax base onto consumption while the largest accumulations of wealth go untaxed [S3].
Retirees and others spending money accumulated under the old income tax would pay the sales tax on consumption that was already taxed when earned, a transition cost the bill does not compensate.
The rebate requires annual registration listing all household members with Social Security numbers, and a family that misses the filing window loses payments until it cures the lapse [S3].

The 23% tax-inclusive rate equals roughly a 30% markup at checkout, and whether that rate actually replaces all the revenue from the taxes being repealed is disputed; the bill fixes the general-revenue component at 14.91% with the rest of the rate dedicated to Social Security and Medicare trust funds [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill makes a real promise to ordinary people — no income tax filing, no payroll withholding, and a rebate that removes federal tax from poverty-level spending — and its self-sunset clause is an unusual safeguard against ending up with both an income tax and a sales tax. But the distributional arithmetic is the serious problem: eliminating taxes on investment income and estates concentrates the largest gains at the top, while the replacement tax falls on consumption, which weighs most heavily on the middle of the income scale and doubly taxes retirees living off past savings. Whether the prebate fully offsets that depends entirely on where a family sits relative to the poverty line. A honest reading is that the bill trades a progressive tax code for a flat consumption tax with a floor under the poorest households, and the biggest beneficiaries are those with the most accumulated wealth.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced and sat there, with no hearing, markup, or floor vote, until the 114th Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on January 6, 2015, and referred the same day to the House Ways and Means Committee [S5].
No further action of any kind appears in the record for the rest of the two-year Congress [S5].
The bill carried 76 cosponsors, all of them Republicans, with no Democratic support [S4].
The same fate is standard for sweeping tax-replacement proposals: with no hearing or markup ever scheduled, the bill died quietly when the Congress ended.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The existing tax system and the interests attached to it — the IRS, the tax preparation and estate-planning professions, and the current distribution of tax burdens — continued unchanged; no household's taxes moved at all.

sides.party_line_note: All 76 cosponsors were Republicans and the sponsor was a Republican; no Democrat signed on, and the bill never reached a floor vote where a roll call could be recorded [S4].

industries.note: The bill repeals the income tax on wages, dividends, and capital gains, the payroll tax on high earnings, and the estate and gift tax, and exempts property bought for investment from the sales tax. The replacement tax falls on consumption, which is a larger share of income for ordinary families, so the shift moves the tax burden away from the top.

industries.industry: Tax preparation, tax software, and estate-planning professions
industries.note: Repealing the income tax and cutting off IRS funding after 2019 would eliminate most individual and business tax filing and much estate-planning work. Consumers would no longer pay for those services, so the industry's loss runs alongside the public's gain here.

Retailers must register, collect and remit the tax, maintain segregated accounts, and large sellers must post bonds, but they receive an administration credit of at least $200 or 0.25% of taxes remitted and shed income tax compliance. Whether the new checkout tax depresses their sales is the open question.

States with sales taxes may administer the federal tax and keep a 0.25% fee on collections, converting their existing sales tax machinery into a revenue stream, though they must meet federal remittance deadlines under penalty of losing the role.
